video_title: Is America’s Strategy in Iran Backfiring? with Robert Pape | TGS 235
gist: University of Chicago political scientist Robert Pape argues the US-Iran war has entered the 'trap' stage of an escalation trap: Iran now uses cheap drones and mines to selectively control Hormuz and, after the Ansar Allah strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, is squeezing the Red Sea bypass too, taking Middle East exports from ~25 to ~13.5 million barrels a day. He warns the next steps (possible Iranian nuclear tests, US tactical nukes on Pickaxe Mountain) could hit Gulf petrodollar recycling into US Treasuries, with 10-year yields already at 5%, and that the US is sliding from preeminence toward being a Western Hemisphere regional power unless it moves to offshore balancing.

themes.theme: Oil supply shock and Red Sea bypass fragility

insights.claim: After Ansar Allah attacked Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline in September 2026, Middle East oil exports reportedly fell from about 25 million barrels a day to about 13.5 million, cutting world supply from roughly 100 to about 88 million barrels a day, with the gap being met by drawing on storage.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: A roughly 12% global supply hole covered by inventories cannot last, so watch storage draws and time spreads for signs the buffer is running out.
insights.quote: what was 25 million barrels a day of exports to the world are down to around 13 and a half million

insights.claim: Robert Pape says the East-West pipeline attack hit eight separate aim points and can be repaired without specialized equipment (Hagens cites at least six weeks), but a repaired pipeline stays highly exposed to repeat strikes by Iraqi Iran-backed militias, the Houthis, Iran itself or ground saboteurs, much like Allied rail bombing in WWII that had to be repeated over and over.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Do not treat a pipeline repair date as a supply-restoration date. Red Sea export capacity carries a lasting risk premium because it can be hit again.
insights.quote: if they repair them, they are hyper-vulnerable to being hit again

insights.claim: Nate Hagens suggests Saudi Arabia may choose not to repair the East-West pipeline, or may repair it but keep it shut until some deal is struck, because drones could simply take it down again.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Saudi Red Sea export volumes may depend on a political deal rather than on engineering, which stretches the likely length of the outage.

insights.claim: Pape identifies three cushions that softened the Hormuz disruption, and says all of them are temporary and shrinking: strategic petroleum reserve releases by the US and 31 other countries, China cutting about 5 million barrels a day of demand after its summit with Trump (quid pro quo still unknown), and roughly 5 million barrels a day rerouted through the East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Track each cushion (SPR levels, Chinese import demand, Yanbu loadings) as a separate indicator. The price shock gets worse as each one runs out.
insights.quote: These are not permanent, and this is based on twenty years of modeling the bombing of Iran

insights.claim: Pape warns that even if the Red Sea pipeline stays open, attackers could strike a giant refinery he places near Yanbu (he names Abqaiq) and knock out that oil anyway, so the Saudi bypass has always been highly vulnerable.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Saudi refining and export terminals are more tail-risk targets. Refined-product cracks could spike even without new pipeline damage.

insights.claim: Nate Hagens says a 'pig in the python' shortage of crude and refined products is coming even if the war ended immediately, citing oil at $135 a barrel in Shanghai and US diesel at $6.50 a gallon while inventories are still being drawn down.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Product tightness lags the physical disruption, so diesel and refined-product prices may stay high after any ceasefire. Be wary of fading energy on peace headlines.
insights.quote: there's a pig in the python coming with global crude and refined products

insights.claim: Hagens argues that modern culture is 'energy blind', assuming oil will be more plentiful and affordable every year, and that this assumption is now being knocked away.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Macro models and valuations that assume cheap, growing energy supply may be structurally mispriced.

insights.claim: A large share of the world's remaining oil reserves sits close to Iran (Hagens says about half of recoverable oil within about 500 miles, Pape says over half of reserves within about a 150-mile radius), which is why US policy since the 1970s has aimed to prevent any single oil hegemon, whether the Soviet Union, Iraq, Iran or Saudi Arabia.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Geographic concentration makes the Gulf a single point of failure for world oil. Iranian regional control is a structural energy risk, not a passing headline.

themes.theme: Escalation trap and Iran's maximum leverage

insights.claim: Pape's 'escalation trap' model has three stages: (1) the attacker bombs and wins tactically, killing leaders; (2) the target does not collapse but gains power, a strategic failure for the attacker; (3) the trap itself, where the attacker cannot walk away and keeps weighing more escalation. He says the US is now in stage three with Iran.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Under this model the base case is continued escalation rather than resolution, so avoid positioning for a quick peace dividend.
insights.quote: there's a stage two where the other side doesn't collapse and gains power

insights.claim: In a June 15 post Pape predicted Iran would enter a period of 'maximum leverage' from mid-July: the US-Iran MoU would break almost immediately, a second front would open in the Red Sea, and Iran's demands would expand to fully evicting American forces from the region. He says all of this has since happened.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Pape's calls have a track record in this conflict, so his forward calls (nuclear tests, more pressure on the bypasses) deserve weight in scenario planning.
insights.quote: Iran is about to come into a period of maximum leverage

insights.claim: Pape says Iran has moved from responding to violence to initiating it and widening its sphere of influence, and that the Houthi attacks were a 72-hour spurt at the end of a ramp-up that began around July 20.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: The pipeline strike is part of a coordinated campaign, not a one-off, so more attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure should be expected.
insights.quote: you are watching a coherence Iran strategy. It's rolling out bit by bit since July

insights.claim: Pape says Iran controls Hormuz through the 'Second Precision Revolution', using cheap mass drones combined with mines to selectively let through only its own ships or those that cut a deal. This orchestrated on/off control turns disruption into political power, which is different from a blunt blockade.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Hormuz flows now depend on political deals made ship by ship, so watch which countries and shippers strike transit deals with Tehran.
insights.quote: You can turn it off and turn it on. That's what generates power.

insights.claim: Pape argues Iran waited for the US and Israel to attack first (in June 2025 and again in February 2026) before closing Hormuz, so blame for the economic damage lands on Washington. He says global opinion polls now blame America and Trump more than Israel.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: The US is losing diplomatic goodwill, which weakens coalition support for US policy and reduces foreign appetite for US assets.
insights.quote: Iran waited until we attacked

insights.claim: Pape says the US cannot simply walk away as it did from Vietnam, because leaving would cede control of about 20% of world energy to an Iran that would then expand further. That is why the escalation debate keeps coming back.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: The chance of a quick US withdrawal that normalizes flows is low, which argues for a lasting Gulf risk premium in oil.
insights.quote: Here, you walk, and this is what you're seeing. Iran expands.

insights.claim: Pape says Iran's next likely escalation is one or two nuclear tests, possibly in October 2026 as an 'October surprise', though it could slip to November or January.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: This is a specific tail-risk window for oil, gold, defense stocks and risk assets in Q4 2026.
insights.quote: The next thing you're seriously gonna think about doing is doing, uh, one or two, maybe two nuclear tests in October.

insights.claim: Pape reports that people in the US administration have for weeks been seriously discussing tactical nuclear weapons against Iran's Pickaxe Mountain site, and reads a recent CSIS report on increased activity there as preparing the public for future operations.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: US nuclear first use would be a regime-change-level shock for global markets. Watch official briefings on Pickaxe Mountain as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: there are people, quote, in the administration thinking seriously about tactical nuclear weapons against Pickaxe Mountain

insights.claim: Pape argues Iran is in a 'win-win' position on the tactical-nuke question: if the US uses one on Pickaxe Mountain, it breaks the 80-year nuclear taboo and deepens the escalation trap rather than ending it.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Markets should not price a US nuclear strike as war-ending. Pape expects it to escalate further and speed up US isolation.
insights.quote: Iran is in a win-win here

insights.claim: Pape says Trump has a consistent coercive strategy, punishment, used with every tool: leadership decapitation, then bombing, then the April 12 economic blockade of Iran, and also with tariffs and at home. Each step widens the pain in the hope the target caves.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Expect US policy to escalate costs rather than change course, across trade as well as war, which is a predictable pattern for tariff and sanctions risk.
insights.quote: Punishment is his strategy.

insights.claim: Pape defines strategy as action, then mechanism, then outcome, and says the mechanism is what matters: raising costs on an opponent produces fight or flight, not cooperation. That is why Iran has not caved over six and a half months.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: This is a reusable lens for judging any sanctions, tariff or blockade campaign: punishment-based coercion rarely produces a negotiated deal.
insights.quote: when you drive up costs on somebody, you get a fight or flight, but you don't get cooperation

insights.claim: Pape argues US punishment is rallying Iranian society behind the IRGC and making a government that was unpopular with most Iranians more popular, the same backlash seen when Germany's bombing of London led Britain to install Bomber Harris and plan firebombing of 58 German towns.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Regime collapse or popular capitulation in Iran is unlikely, so a durable adversary means a longer conflict and sustained energy disruption.
insights.quote: We're making the Iran government popular.

insights.claim: Pape says administrations rarely model the worst case that actually hits them. He notes that on March 2, two days after the Supreme Leader was killed, Trump said there was no real worst case and mentioned neither Hormuz nor Pickaxe Mountain.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Policymakers systematically underestimate tail risks, so investors should not rely on official reassurance when judging geopolitical tails.
insights.quote: they don't develop the worst case that actually happened to them

insights.claim: Pape says the MoU approach led by J.D. Vance treated Iran as a business negotiation over a price, when Iran is pursuing great-power politics and wants power, including financial power, not just money.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of headlines about transactional deals ending the war. Pape expects any accord to be fragile unless it concedes power.
insights.quote: this is not a business deal. This is great power politics of the first order

themes.theme: Petrodollar recycling and US Treasury demand

insights.claim: Pape argues Iran's pressure on the Gulf governments that host US bases (Kuwait, Iraq, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia) aims to shake them enough that their central banks stop buying US Treasuries with petrodollars, and possibly sell Treasuries at Iran's direction. He says this will squeeze US seigniorage 'until there's a pop'.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: A weaker Gulf bid for Treasuries puts upward pressure on long-end yields and the term premium. Watch TIC data on Gulf holdings.
insights.quote: it's gonna squeeze that seigniorage, Nate, until there's a pop

insights.claim: US long-end yields are already stressed: Hagens notes the 10-year Treasury hit 5% for the first time in decades, Pape cites the 30-year near 5.3% against about $40 trillion of US debt, and they agree yields of 8-9% would kill the economy.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: The fiscal position is vulnerable to any geopolitical hit on foreign demand for Treasuries, which is a duration risk.
insights.quote: Yesterday 10-year notes hit 5% for the first time in, in decades.

insights.claim: Pape warns that US use of tactical nuclear weapons would damage Treasury auctions, because foreign buyers angry at a 'pariah' America could demand much higher yields. He rejects the idea that the world will always buy US bonds.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Geopolitical escalation could show up as weak 10- and 30-year auctions, adding a political-risk premium to US duration.
insights.quote: people are saying, "Oh, no, they'll always buy our bonds, you know. They, they need us." I, I'm telling you, this is too dangerous.

insights.claim: Pape says that once Iran controls Persian Gulf oil flows, its next goal is financial power. He notes Iran's president told a recent BRICS summit that Iran wants oil traded in a basket of currencies, not yuan alone.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Energy de-dollarization via a currency basket is a slow but real threat to dollar demand. Watch BRICS settlement mechanisms.
insights.quote: We're not looking for, uh, the oil to be traded in yuan alone. We're looking for some sort of basket of currencies.

insights.claim: Pape says Saudi Crown Prince MBS pushed Trump and Netanyahu toward the February 28 regime-change strike (as reported by The New York Times), then after April refused US use of Saudi airspace in an attempt to move toward neutrality, a hedge Pape says 'was never gonna work'.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Saudi Arabia is exposed on both sides, a target for Iran and a less reliable US partner, so Saudi political risk is rising.
insights.quote: This was never gonna work, Nate.

insights.claim: Pape sees a real chance that Iran works covertly with Saudi tribes and leaders unhappy with the House of Saud to push for a friendlier government in Riyadh, comparable to Putin's aim in Kyiv. He considers this worse for Saudi Arabia than a negotiated Saudi-Iran deal.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Saudi regime-stability risk is a low-probability, high-impact tail for oil supply and for Gulf sovereign asset allocation.

themes.theme: US military vulnerability and superpower decline

insights.claim: Pape says the 13 US bases in the Persian Gulf, supported by about 50,000 troops, have been severely damaged and partly obliterated (which he says a Pentagon report that morning admitted), the Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain was pummeled, and the carrier Abraham Lincoln had to go back to Diego Garcia to resupply.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: The US can no longer project force cheaply in the Gulf, which weakens its ability to secure shipping lanes and supports a higher oil risk premium.
insights.quote: those thirteen air bases have been severely damaged, parts of them obliterated

insights.claim: Pape says Iran is now threatening US carriers with Mach 5 missiles that Aegis-class cruisers cannot stop, so the US position in the Gulf has shifted from preeminence to vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Hypersonic and cheap-drone warfare undermines legacy naval platforms, which matters for defense procurement priorities and defense stocks.
insights.quote: we've gone from a position of near preeminence to a position of vulnerability

insights.claim: Pape warns that on its current path the US would have to retreat from superpower status to being a regional power in the Western Hemisphere, but says this is not yet inevitable and a new approach may become possible from January 2027, after the midterms lengthen leaders' time horizons.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Post-midterm policy could be a turning point, so watch for a shift in US Middle East strategy in early 2027.
insights.quote: we're gonna have to pull back and be happy with being a regional power in the Western Hemisphere

insights.claim: Pape says allies now doubt America's capability, not just its will. EU parliamentarians see the US as incapable of supporting Ukraine, and he expects South Korea and Japan are having the same conversation. The result is more power vacuums and a far more conflict-prone world.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Doubts about US capability point to allied rearmament and higher defense budgets in Europe and Asia.
insights.quote: This is America incapable of supporting Ukraine. That's a different world.

insights.claim: Pape argues that 35 years of globalization rested on US protection established by the 1991 Gulf War: countries cut military budgets and leaned on trade because stability made it cheaper. He says that arrangement is now reversing.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: A reversal of globalization means structurally higher defense spending, reshoring and supply-chain redundancy, which is inflationary for the macro regime.
insights.quote: for thirty-five years, we have had what's called globalization

insights.claim: Pape says Iranian leader Arachi's trips to Moscow and Beijing in April and May produced talk of a 'new security architecture' that excludes the US, and that China wants the US to lose so that Washington cannot control the Hormuz oil that flows to China.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: A Russia-China-Iran energy and security bloc could reroute Gulf energy flows eastward and reduce US leverage over global oil.
insights.quote: a new security architecture

insights.claim: Pape, researching a new book, notes that strong powers launching preventive wars (Germany before both World Wars, Japan before WWII, Russia against Ukraine in 2022, and now the US against Iran) have repeatedly suffered disaster, which he attributes to the hubris that comes with preeminent power.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: History suggests the dominant power's overconfidence is itself a risk factor, so be wary of assuming US strength guarantees a favorable outcome.
insights.quote: all those countries launched preventive wars that turned out to be disastrous for them

insights.claim: Pape's best-case path is a multi-year offshore-balancing strategy aimed at regional stability rather than regime change or withdrawal. Local actors would carry most of the load and the US would do only about 20% of the military heavy lifting.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: A US pivot to offshore balancing would take years, so the region stays unstable in the meantime, while Gulf defense procurement would rise.
insights.quote: the goal becomes not regime change and not walking away, but regional stability

insights.claim: Pape cites two precedents for offshore balancing. ISIS was defeated mainly by ground forces (about 80%) with US air power in a supporting role over four years, and Ukraine resists Russia because the US spent years from 2014 helping it build a professional officer corps, not because of dollar aid or Javelins.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: Military effectiveness comes from professional mid-level officers and logistics rather than hardware counts, which is useful for judging how well defense aid will work.
insights.quote: what beat ISIS was eighty percent the ground elements

insights.claim: Pape argues the Gulf states, especially Saudi Arabia and the UAE, are fully capable of running drone operations and should enforce the blockade of Iranian tankers themselves instead of the costly US Navy mission, with US military advisors helping them build real militaries.
insights.speaker: Robert Pape
insights.so_what: This implies more Gulf spending on drones, military training and advisory services as the US tries to hand off regional security.
insights.quote: The Saudis, perfectly capable of running drone technology.
